segments.sec: Start Here: AI Basics
segments.say: Lesson 3. What is an L L M & How You Use One. Next-token prediction, how chat models are trained (pretraining leads to instruction tuning leads to R L H F), and what an L L M A P I call actually looks like.

segments.sec: The basics
segments.say: A large language model (L L M) is a huge neural network trained on enormous amounts of text to do one thing: predict the next token. Chatting, coding and summarising all emerge from repeating that prediction over and over. Here is an analogy. Your phone keyboard's next-word suggestion, scaled up enormously: trained on a large share of the internet and books, with billions of weights, until its "next word" guesses can write essays and code.

segments.sec: The basics
segments.say: Why does this matter? Every A I engineering role builds products on top of L L M A P Is. Knowing how L L Ms are trained explains their strengths (fluency) and weaknesses (hallucination, knowledge cutoff, no memory), which is why rag, tools and evals exist. A few key words. Token: A chunk of text ( about ¾ of a word) that the model reads and writes. Pretraining: Learning next-token prediction on huge raw text. Instruction tuning (S F T): Extra training on question leads to good answer examples. R L H F / preference tuning: Training on human preferences to be helpful and safe. Prompt: The input text/messages you send. Context window: Maximum tokens per request. Hallucination: Confident but false output. Knowledge cutoff: The date after which the model saw no training data.

segments.sec: Watch: Generation = predicting one token at a time
segments.say: Generation equals predicting one token at a time. You give the model some text. It doesn't "look up" an answer; it scores every possible next token.

segments.sec: Watch: Generation = predicting one token at a time
segments.say: Probabilities over its whole vocabulary (~100k tokens). "Paris" is by far the most likely, because it has seen this pattern many times in training.

segments.sec: Watch: Generation = predicting one token at a time
segments.say: Pick a token (sampling) and append it to the text.

segments.sec: Watch: Generation = predicting one token at a time
segments.say: . then predict again with the longer text. Repeat until a stop token or max tokens. That's all generation is: a loop of next-token predictions.

segments.sec: Watch: Generation = predicting one token at a time
segments.say: Because it predicts what sounds right rather than checking facts, it can produce fluent but false answers: hallucinations. Grounding with rag reduces this.

segments.sec: Watch: From text predictor to chat assistant
segments.say: From text predictor to chat assistant. Pretraining: the network reads a huge amount of text and learns to predict the next token. This is where its knowledge and language skill come from. It costs months and millions of dollars.

segments.sec: Watch: From text predictor to chat assistant
segments.say: The result is a base model: excellent at continuing text, but it doesn't reliably follow instructions. Ask it a question and it may just add more questions.

segments.sec: Watch: From text predictor to chat assistant
segments.say: Instruction tuning (S F T): train further on curated examples of instructions paired with ideal answers.

segments.sec: Watch: From text predictor to chat assistant
segments.say: Preference tuning (R L H F / D P O): humans or A I judges rank answers, and the model learns to prefer helpful, honest, harmless ones.

segments.sec: Watch: From text predictor to chat assistant
segments.say: The chat model you call through an A P I. Notice what it still lacks: your private data, events after the cutoff, memory between calls and real-world actions. Those gaps are why the rest of this course exists.

segments.sec: Watch: What an API call looks like
segments.say: What an A P I call looks like. Your code sends a request: which model, a list of messages (a system instruction plus the conversation), and settings like max tokens and temperature.

segments.sec: Watch: What an API call looks like
segments.say: The provider runs the forward pass token by token on G P Us (you can stream tokens as they're produced).

segments.sec: Watch: What an API call looks like
segments.say: You get back the generated text plus usage (input and output tokens), which is what you're billed for.

segments.sec: Watch: What an API call looks like
segments.say: Crucially, the A P I is stateless: it remembers nothing. For a follow-up question you resend the whole conversation. Managing that is "memory" (a later lesson).

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: Message roles. system: instructions and persona, for example "You are a support bot. Only answer from the docs.". user: what the human said. assistant: what the model said earlier (you send this back to keep conversation history). tool results: outputs of functions the model asked to call (agents lesson).

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: Core limitations leads to what solves them. Doesn't know your private or recent data leads to rag. Can't take actions or fetch live data leads to tool calling / agents. No memory between calls leads to memory / context engineering. Can be wrong or unsafe leads to evals and guardrails. Cost and latency leads to serving, caching, routing. That's the roadmap of this whole app.

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: Closed versus open-weight models. Closed (Claude, G P T, Gemini): use via A P I, strongest models, no infrastructure to run. Open-weight (Llama, Mistral, Qwen. ): download and self-host, with full control and data residency, but you run the G P Us.

segments.sec: Learn
segments.say: Say it in the interview. "An L L M is a transformer trained to predict the next token, first by pretraining on massive text, then aligned with instruction tuning and preference optimisation into a chat model. We use it through a stateless A P I with system and user messages, paying per token. Its gaps (private data, freshness, actions, memory, reliability) are what rag, tools, memory and evals address.".

segments.sec: Compare
segments.say: Let's compare. Trained with: pretraining only, plus S F T plus preference tuning. Behaviour: continues text, follows instructions, converses. Use: research, further fine-tuning, apps, agents, assistants.

segments.sec: Compare
segments.say: Closed versus open-weight. Examples: Claude, G P T, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen. Setup: A P I key, G P Us plus serving stack. Control / privacy: provider terms, full control. Typical use: fastest path to quality, data residency, high steady volume, customisation.

segments.sec: Interview recall
segments.say: A likely interview question: What is an L L M, and what can't it do on its own? A strong answer: A transformer trained to predict the next token, then aligned into a chat assistant. On its own it lacks your private and fresh data, can't take actions, has no memory between calls, and can hallucinate. rag, tools, memory and evals fill those gaps.
